ask: Hi. Sorry. I’m after a book about a whale. It’s old, and the captain’s got a wooden leg. It starts, “Call me Ahab.”

books.label: Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea

wrong: No, it’s longer than that. Much longer. There’s a whole chapter just about the colour white.
No. Old, enormous, a whale, and that chapter about white.
found: That’s it. It’s huge. “Call me Ishmael.” Who’s Ishmael?
more: It starts “Call me Ishmael”: the one telling it. Ahab’s the one who won’t stop. People keep the loudest name in a book and lose the one who was telling it to them.
tine: Everybody stops at the chapter on whiteness. Read it on a train, where you can’t get up and do something else.

ask: It’s for my son, for school. The one where a man wakes up and he’s turned into a beetle. It’s called Metamorphosis, I know that much.
wrong: No, it’s thinner than that. He’s a travelling salesman, and he wakes up worried he’s going to miss his train.
No. Thin, a salesman, the train. And the beetle.
found: That’s the one. Look how thin it is. He’ll still say it’s too long.
more: Kafka never says beetle. He says ungeheueres Ungeziefer, a monstrous vermin, and he wrote to his publisher that the insect itself mustn’t be drawn on the cover. I only ever had his words, never a cover, so I may be one of the few who never saw the beetle.
tine: Tell him the beetle’s the easy part. It’s the family that’s frightening.

ask: I had a book as a boy. Three boys shipwrecked on an island. Ralph, and Jack, and one more. All frightfully decent to one another. My grandson says it ends horribly. I don’t remember it ending horribly.
wrong: No. Nobody’s called Piggy, and nobody’s called Jim. Mine was old already when I had it.
No, no. Older. Kinder. Ralph, Jack, and the third one, the funny one.
found: That’s it! Ralph, Jack and Peterkin. Peterkin. I’d forgotten him entirely.
more: Both are real, and both have a Ralph and a Jack: Golding took the names from this one on purpose, to say boys on an island wouldn’t be like that. This man had the first as a boy, his grandson has the second, and he’d made them one book. That’s most of remembering wrong: two true things, kept as one.
tine: Read them both, one after the other. Then tell your grandson which boys you’d rather be stuck with.

ask: A little book. For children, but not really. A boy on a tiny planet, and a drawing that looks like a hat, but it’s a snake that’s swallowed an elephant. The Little Princess, I think.
wrong: No, not that one. Mine has a fox in it, who wants to be tamed. And a rose under a glass.
No. The fox, the rose, the little planet.
found: Prince. Of course it’s Prince. I read it in French at school and cried on the bus.
more: Nearly everyone who asks for it gets the title a little wrong and the elephant exactly right. In the book, every grown-up the narrator shows it to sees a hat.
tine: Grown-ups buy that one for a child, read it on the way home, and keep it.

ask: I want the Sherlock Holmes where he says, “Elementary, my dear Watson.” I’d like to see it on the page. I’ve been saying it for fifty years.

books.label: Conan Doyle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles
Conan Doyle, The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
It isn’t in any of them

wrong: Not in that one? Try another. He says it all the time.
Not there either? I’d have sworn to it.
Well, it must be in that one, then.
found: Not in any of them? Fifty years. Well. I’ll take the one where he nearly does.
more: He never says it. “Elementary,” once, in The Crooked Man, and “my dear Watson” often, but never in one breath: the films put them together. Some days the most useful thing I can tell someone is that it isn’t there.
tine: The Crooked Man, in the Memoirs. He says “Elementary,” and stops. Don’t pencil the rest in. I’ll know.
